conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be overseeing your care tonight. Can you tell me why you’re here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’m here to get my abatacept infusion for psoriatic arthritis, but last time I had it, I had a bad reaction—shortness of breath, chest tightness, like an asthma attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were premedicated with higher-dose prednisone starting yesterday, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been on 80 mg prednisone since yesterday instead of my usual 40 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re also giving you 100 mg of methylprednisolone before the infusion, plus Benadryl and famotidine to reduce the risk of another reaction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’m a bit nervous though—what if it happens again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. That’s why we’re doing this in the hospital with close monitoring. If anything happens, we’ll treat it right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll stay overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you for 24 hours after the infusion just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your premedications—Benedryl and famotidine. The abatacept will begin in about 45 minutes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I feel fine so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting the abatacept now. It will run over 90 minutes. We’ll be watching you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I can feel the IV starting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, my hand and arm are swelling and turning red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that. We’re giving you an IV dose of Benadryl to help with this. It should improve quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a mild reaction, and we’re treating it. You’re stable, but we’ll keep monitoring closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My chest feels tight again, like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you an albuterol nebulizer treatment with Atrovent to open your airways. Just relax and breathe slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest tightness is improving. Your oxygen levels are normal, and your lungs sound clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here for that. You’re responding well to treatment. We’ll keep the observation going through the night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got your blood work back. Your white count is a bit high at 14.2, but that’s likely from the steroids. Everything else looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a concern?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not in this case. Steroids often raise white blood cells. Your kidney and liver values are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve passed the 24-hour mark since the infusion and remain stable. We’ll continue your current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m doing okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The reaction you had was manageable, and we prevented it from getting worse. You’ll continue prednisone at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need this level of monitoring every time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your allergist recommended this protocol, so it may be repeated for future doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re still doing well. We’re planning to discharge you later today if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my diabetes and blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your oral diabetes meds during the infusion and used insulin instead. You’ll go back to glyburide at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We paused them during monitoring, but you’ll restart lisinopril, hydrochlorothiazide, and Toprol at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for explaining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable overnight. We’re ready to discharge you. You’ll continue the new prednisone dose and all your other medications as listed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No changes to my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only temporary changes during the infusion. Everything else returns to your usual regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have another reaction at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER if you have swelling, trouble breathing, rash, or chest tightness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you tolerated it as well as you did. Follow up with your rheumatologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You can leave in about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Here’s your discharge summary. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having some neck swelling and pain since your recent surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I had the fistulotomy two days ago, and my throat was sore after the procedure. It got better at first, but then yesterday the pain came back worse, and now my neck is swollen and red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And are you having any trouble swallowing or breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can swallow, but it hurts. Liquids are easier. No trouble breathing, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. You don’t have fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever. Just the pain and swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ER, they did a laryngoscopy and saw some swelling in your vocal cords. They’re concerned about an infection in your right submandibular gland.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The salivary gland under the jaw? What’s causing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to your recent intubation. Sometimes trauma from the breathing tube can cause inflammation or blockage in the duct, leading to infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that makes sense. They said it was a difficult intubation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ve ordered a CT scan to get a better look. We’ll also start you on antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. What kind of antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Clindamycin. It covers the kinds of bacteria we’re worried about, especially since you’re on immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’m on prednisone and azathioprine for my psoriatic arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that’s why we’re being cautious. Your immune system isn’t responding as strongly, so infections can spread faster.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan is back. It shows inflammation in the right submandibular gland, with some fluid and small pockets of air. This suggests sialadenitis — an infection of the salivary gland.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious? Could it turn into something worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small concern it could progress to Ludwig’s angina, which is a deeper neck infection, but right now the airway is open and there’s no abscess. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue clindamycin, use warm compresses, and encourage saliva flow with lemon drops or sipping water. ENT will also help express the gland to drain some fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. And my other meds — should I keep taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep taking your prednisone and azathioprine. But your rheumatologist advised holding off on starting Humira until after you finish antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I wasn’t planning to start it yet anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed some white patches in your mouth during the exam. Could be thrush, a fungal infection, common with steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I’ve had that before. Should I start antifungal treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start clotrimazole troches four times a day. We’ll reassess in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still pretty painful. The swelling hasn’t gone down much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your white blood cell count is elevated, which means the infection is still active. We’re going to repeat the CT to see if there’s any change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a bad sign?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It just means we need to make sure the treatment is working. The repeat CT will help us decide if we need to adjust anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The new CT shows the fluid collection has gotten a bit larger — it’s now a superinfected sialocele. But no abscess, and no spread to deeper spaces.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what does that mean for treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue the same antibiotics and supportive care. ENT will come by to express the gland again. Sometimes that helps relieve pressure and speed healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the thrush? The troches seem to be helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. The patches are improving. We’ll keep it on for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You look better. The swelling is starting to go down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it feels a bit better. I can swallow more easily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your WBC has come down from 16 to 14 — still high, but improving. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re eating and drinking well, and that the infection keeps improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ENT was able to express some fluid from the gland earlier. That should help with healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It did feel like some pressure was released.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep doing warm compresses and sialogogues. Also, your blood sugar has been running high — up to 248 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, steroids do that to me. Should I adjust my glyburide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added glyburide to your inpatient meds. We’ll keep monitoring it. You’ll continue it at home as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Afebrile, eating, pain much improved. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full 7-day course of clindamycin. Use warm compresses and lemon drops. Take pain meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the clotrimazole?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop that — no signs of thrush today. Follow up with ENT in a week. If swelling comes back, or you have trouble breathing, go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your usual regimen. Prednisone at a lower dose, azathioprine, blood pressure and diabetes meds. We’ve adjusted some doses — all listed in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of a severe headache. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started yesterday in the back of my head and now it’s all over. It feels just like my usual flare-ups when my psoriatic arthritis gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned you tried morphine at home. Did it help at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I took my regular dose—30 mg twice and 15 mg twice—but it didn’t touch the pain. That’s when I called rheumatology, and they told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. No fever, neck stiffness, or vision changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. Just the headache and some swelling in my hands and feet, which also happens when my disease flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. In the ER, you got IV morphine and steroids. How’s the pain now compared to earlier?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still there. The IV meds helped a lot, but I know it’ll come back if we don’t do something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on your prednisone and azathioprine. The rheumatology team reviewed your case and doesn’t think increasing steroids will help long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been on prednisone for over a year now. I’m just waiting on approval for Humira, but it’s taking forever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The pain team is also involved. They’re thinking about an occipital nerve block tomorrow to help break this cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of that. Is it safe? I’ve had Botox before, but it never got approved for me this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very safe. They’ll inject a numbing medicine and a steroid around the nerves at the base of your skull. It often gives good relief for cervicogenic headaches like yours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m willing to try it. My headaches are always worse when my immune suppression is low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And we’re not seeing signs of infection—no fever or meningismus—so this seems like a flare, not something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I also started Augmentin for an axillary abscess a few days ago. Is that okay to keep taking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue that for the full 7-day course. No signs of spreading infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your headache today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little less intense. I slept okay after the last dose of morphine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs from last night were stable. White count is normal, though neutrophils are high, which we expect from long-term steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had that before. What’s the plan for today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling the nerve block for tomorrow morning. In the meantime, we’ll keep your pain managed with oral morphine and monitor your response.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes? I’m on glargine and sliding scale. Should I keep that up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue glargine 50 in the morning and 30 at night. We’re holding glyburide for now since steroids can raise your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure meds—Toprol, HCTZ, lisinopril—I should keep those too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual meds except glyburide. We’re also keeping your Bactrim for PJP prevention because of your immunosuppression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team confirmed—the nerve block is scheduled for tomorrow at noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Any restrictions before the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just stay on your regular diet. They’ll use local anesthesia, so no fasting needed. You’ll be awake but comfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The nerve block is about to start. They’ll inject numbing medicine and a steroid into the occipital nerves on both sides.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready. I hope this helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All done. No complications. You’ll start to feel relief in a few hours, though it might take a day or two for full effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel a bit looser in the neck. That’s promising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good sign. We’re discharging you today. Your pain is stable on oral meds, and you’re otherwise doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes to my meds? I saw some adjustments in the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re cutting some doses—like lowering your metoprolol and HCTZ—because your blood pressure has been stable. Prednisone stays at 50 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the morphine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with sustained-release morphine every 12 hours and the immediate-release as needed. Take it as prescribed, and don’t drive while on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Should I follow up with pain clinic again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially if headaches return. The nerve block may help, but long-term, the pain clinic can explore other options like Botox if approved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And rheumatology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue working on getting Humira approved. No changes to your azathioprine or other meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Augmentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the full course—four more days. It’s for the recurring axillary abscess, and we want to make sure it clears.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar checks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep doing four fingersticks a day. Resume glyburide as planned unless your sugars run low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thanks for getting me through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call your doctor if headaches worsen or aren’t controlled. Otherwise, follow up as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’ll be discharged in the next hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel. I’ve reviewed your chart. You came in today because of exhaustion and heavy sweating—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago. I woke up drenched in sweat, even though I wasn’t hot. It’s been happening every day since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you mentioned feeling completely wiped out—how long have you been feeling that way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About three days. I slept 17 hours straight the other night and still felt exhausted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve also been on Humira, azathioprine, and prednisone for your psoriatic arthritis and IBD. Did your symptoms start around the time of your last Humira dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Now that you mention it—yes, the sweating started the morning after my last injection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Given your immunosuppression, we’re concerned about infection, but also possible side effects from your medications. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a fever, though. My temperature usually runs low—around 96.3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s noted. We’ll still check for infections like CMV, EBV, and others. We’ve already done blood work and a chest X-ray—both were normal so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been having more joint pain in the mornings—worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s part of what we’re monitoring. We’ll keep you on prednisone for now. We’ve held your Humira and azathioprine temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop them completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re waiting on more test results. If we confirm this is a reaction to Humira, we may discontinue it permanently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CMV and EBV tests came back negative. Blood cultures show no growth so far. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about the calf pain I’ve been having?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound—no sign of a blood clot. But we noticed a red, tender lump on your right calf. Dermatology thinks it might be erythema nodosum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an inflammatory condition, often linked to autoimmune diseases like yours. We’ll biopsy it to confirm, but it’s not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually, yes—especially once we manage the underlying trigger. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve completed a CT scan of your chest, abdomen, and pelvis. No signs of infection or cancer. Your liver shows fatty infiltration, which we already knew about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing’s showing up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing concerning. Your symptoms are likely related to your immune system—possibly a reaction to Humira. We’re leaning toward stopping it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been nauseous after meals—could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. With your IBD history and family background, we’re watching that. But it’s likely stable—nothing acute.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture and fungal tests are back—no infection. Toxoplasmosis and mycoplasma were negative too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the pending ones—Aspergillus, coccidioides?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still pending, but given your negative CT and blood work, the chance of those is very low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another CT of your neck—no signs of infection or swelling. The old sialocele is still there, but not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my headaches—they’ve been worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. You were supposed to get Botox, but we held off because we needed to rule out infection first. Botox can cause side effects that mimic illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what can we do now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll consult pain management. They may offer trigger point injections instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your spinal tap came back clean. No infection in the spinal fluid. That’s a big relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No tumors, strokes, or inflammation. Just some old, stable white matter changes—nothing new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So still no explanation for the headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from the scan. But given your history, it’s likely part of your chronic condition. Pain service will see you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy of your calf lesion showed no infection—no bacteria or fungi. Dermatology confirms it’s consistent with erythema nodosum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not dangerous, but it’s a sign your body is inflamed. We’ll restart azathioprine and keep you on prednisone. Humira will be stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Pain service gave you trigger point injections with bupivacaine—no steroid, to avoid confusion with infection symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will that help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should last a few days to weeks. You’ll follow up with them as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been afebrile, stable, and improving. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds should I take?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue prednisone and azathioprine. Stop Humira and Bactrim. We’ve adjusted your morphine and lisinopril doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pending tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A few serologies are still pending. Dermatology will call you with biopsy results. Follow up with rheumatology in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: If I start feeling worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your PCP or come back to the ER if you develop fever, worsening pain, or new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with severe pain in your left leg and knee. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. It started yesterday evening—pins and needles in my left heel, then sharp pain shooting up my calf. Within an hour, it reached my knee. I took morphine at home, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you have a history of psoriatic arthritis, correct? Has it been flaring recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been really bad—swelling in my wrists, knees, toes. I got a steroid shot last week, and things were improving. But this leg pain came back out of nowhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. In the ER, your X-ray showed no fracture, and the ultrasound ruled out a blood clot. We’re going to keep you for pain control and further evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it might be an infection or something serious. I’ve had joint issues before, but this feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. We’re going to check the fluid in your knee to make sure it’s not septic. We’ll do a procedure called arthrocentesis—drawing fluid out with a needle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’ve had that done before. But I’m also stressed—I’m in the middle of a weight-loss and insulin program called 'You Turn.' I was supposed to restart tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll make sure you stay on your insulin and diet. Nutrition is already involved, and you can continue your sliding scale. We’ll help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the arthrocentesis. We removed fluid from your left knee. It looked cloudy, which suggests inflammation, not infection—but we’ll send it to the lab to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected? But why so much pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain is likely from a flare of your psoriatic arthritis. The fluid had a high white blood cell count—58,000—mostly neutrophils. That’s inflammatory, not septic. But we’ll start antibiotics just in case until we get the culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m allergic to Keflex—be careful with the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Noted. We’re using vancomycin and ciprofloxacin—safe for you. We’ll stop them once we confirm no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your joint fluid culture came back negative—no bacteria grew. Blood cultures are also negative so far. We’re stopping the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s just a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re increasing your prednisone from 30mg to 60mg daily to help calm the inflammation. Your rheumatologist agrees with this plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being on high-dose steroids, but I know they help. My blood sugar’s been harder to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. You’re doing well with your insulin sliding scale. Your sugars have been in the 100–140 range—excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve also been sticking to the You Fit diet. I lost 3 pounds already this week!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fantastic. We’ll keep nutrition involved to support you. Now, about your pain—your knee is improving, but you mentioned new calf pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a dull ache now, not sharp. But I know my body—I’ve had erythema nodosum before. This feels like the start of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—an ultrasound of your calf showed no DVT, no abscess, no ruptured Baker’s cyst. There’s mild redness, but no significant swelling or warmth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it still be erythema nodosum? It usually responds to steroids or potassium iodide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But without clear nodules or systemic symptoms, we’re not certain. We’ll keep monitoring. For now, we’re adding gabapentin—your rheumatologist thinks it might help with nerve-type pain or fibromyalgia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your CRP and ESR are elevated—66 and 60—so there’s still inflammation, but your knee is much better. How’s the calf?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still tender. I’m glad the antibiotics are stopped. I was worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. Your cultures remained negative. No sign of infection. We’re continuing the high-dose prednisone for a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other joints? My neck’s been killing me again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your cervical headaches often flare with joint pain. We’ve scheduled a trigger point injection with pain management today—same as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. That usually helps. And my chest pain last night—was that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had substernal pain, but EKG was normal, and it responded to dilaudid. Likely costochondritis—your usual pattern. We’ll keep you on indomethacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just finished the trigger point injection in your neck. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already a bit better. The tightness is easing. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your calf ultrasound today was unchanged—no new fluid or clot. We think the pain is part of your inflammatory flare, not a separate issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not going home with antibiotics or new tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. You’re afebrile, no signs of infection, and improving. We’ll discharge you tomorrow if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my meds? I want to make sure I’m set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re tapering your prednisone to 20mg daily. You’ll continue azathioprine, indomethacin, and now gabapentin three times a day. Your insulin doses are unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the morphine? I still have breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home with sustained-release morphine twice daily and hydromorphone for breakthrough pain—five days' supply.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And compression socks? My legs swell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re sending you home with a pair. Wear them during the day, especially if you’re sitting or standing for long periods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve made great progress. Your knee is much less swollen, and you’re walking better. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I’m ready to get back to my program. But what if the calf pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep an eye on it. If the pain worsens, or you see increasing redness or swelling, call your rheumatologist, ID, or PCP. They may consider more imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up? With rheumatology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have an appointment in one week. They’re also working on getting approval for Cimzia, since Simponi isn’t controlling your disease well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already. I’ll keep up with my diet and insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done an excellent job managing your health. Keep it up. We’ll get your discharge papers ready, and you should be out by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in with left leg pain and swelling. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It started in my heel and shot up to my knee. It's been really painful, and now my calf is red and warm. I just got out of the hospital a day ago for something similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You were treated for a possible septic joint, but tests didn’t show infection, correct? And your prednisone was increased?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. They thought it was a flare of my arthritis. But now this redness and swelling came back, worse than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your ultrasound from earlier today. It shows a large fluid collection in your left calf. It wasn’t there before. We’re concerned this might be an abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An abscess? But I don’t have a fever or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s true, and your vitals are stable. But given your history of psoriatic arthritis and being on immunosuppressants, infections can be subtle. We’re ordering an MRI to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I be worried about surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll decide after the MRI. For now, we’re starting antibiotics—vancomycin and Zosyn—just in case it’s infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your MRI results are in. There are two fluid collections—one in the popliteus muscle and another near the gastrocnemius. They look like small abscesses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they going to drain them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re small, so we may not be able to drain them with a needle. But we’ll monitor closely. Your joint fluid from yesterday showed no infection, so we’re confident it’s not septic arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my arthritis acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be a mix. The redness and swelling suggest cellulitis, and the fluid collections point to abscesses. We’re treating it as an infection for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to aspirate the more superficial part of the abscess to get a sample. It will help us know what we’re dealing with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll numb the area first. You’ll feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It’s important to rule out bacteria like staph.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got about 7 cc of pus from the abscess. It had lots of white blood cells, but no bacteria seen on the gram stain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bacteria? So it’s not infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes cultures take time. We’re keeping you on antibiotics because the fluid and appearance suggest infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures are back—no growth so far. But we’re placing a PICC line so you can get IV antibiotics at home if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A PICC line? Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a long-term IV access. We’ll confirm placement with a chest X-ray. It’ll help you finish a full course of antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray confirms the PICC is in the right spot—good position in the superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But my knee still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s a small fluid collection at the front of your knee, but it’s not infected. Likely inflammation from your psoriatic arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgeons are concerned the abscess isn’t improving. They want to do an incision and drainage tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: More surgery? I just had my knees operated on last year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is minor—just opening the area to let the pus drain. It’ll help you heal faster and reduce the risk of spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. They drained the abscess and left it open to heal from the inside out. You’ll need wound care daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on pain meds, and it should improve. We’ll keep the antibiotics going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest ultrasound shows the main collection is still there but not worse. No sign of DVT, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the bacteria? Did they grow anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still no growth in the cultures. That’s actually common—sometimes antibiotics or your immune system clears it before we catch it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering a muscle biopsy to make sure there’s no unusual infection or inflammation deep in the tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s small. We need to rule out things like fungal or atypical infections, especially since you’re on immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy didn’t show any unusual organisms. No fungus, no TB. Just inflammation and dead tissue—consistent with a resolving abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The antibiotics and drainage helped. We’ll keep the PICC for another week, then switch to oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function has been a bit off. We think it’s from dehydration and the antibiotics. We’re giving you more fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my kidney damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, this looks like acute, reversible change. We’re monitoring it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been a bit confused the last day. We did a brain scan—it’s normal. No stroke or bleed. Likely due to medications or infection effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt foggy. Is it safe to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. Your infection is under control. We’ll keep the PICC for now and arrange home nursing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a fall last night. We checked a head CT—no injury. But we’re reviewing your sedatives. They might be making you drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even remember getting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing your pain meds a bit and watching closely. Safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine and blood cultures are negative. No new infections. We’re confident the abscess is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I walk more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with the walker. Physical therapy will help you regain strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your discharge. You’ll finish IV antibiotics at home for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my rheumatology follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, scheduled in five days. They’ll reassess your immunosuppressants and prednisone dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is draining less. The home health nurse will change the dressing and monitor for signs of worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Fever, increased redness, swelling, or confusion. And keep taking your insulin and gabapentin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. We’ll remove the PICC in two weeks. Keep all your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Call us if anything changes. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your sodium was high earlier. Drink water, but not too much at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep using CPAP for your sleep apnea. It helps healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been using it much in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Start again at home. It’s important for your breathing and heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Any diet changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your diabetic diet. Watch your sugars, especially with prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see you in clinic in two weeks. Call sooner if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep the appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your meds one more time before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—no driving until your pain and sedatives are lower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll have my wife drive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take it slow and heal well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. We’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you came in today because of worsening joint pain, especially on the left side. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. Last night around 6 PM, I started having sharp pain in my left shoulder. It didn’t go away, and by 2 AM, the pain had spread—elbow, fingers, hip, knee, even my toes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you notice any swelling or redness in those joints?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No swelling or redness, but the left knee is especially painful. I’ve also had chills all morning, though no fever that I’ve checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned chills—any cough, shortness of breath, or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I had chest pain last night, but it turned out to be shoulder pain radiating. No breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I see you were recently hospitalized for fluid collections in your left leg. Any changes there now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, the leg hasn’t changed. But my azathioprine was stopped last week, and I think that’s why my joints are flaring up. My last flare like this was over a year ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. You’ve also been on prednisone, which was recently tapered down to 20 mg. That could contribute too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 60 mg before. I felt better then. Could that be why this is happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re thinking this is a flare of your psoriatic arthritis, especially since there’s no sign of infection in your joints or leg wounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not another infection? I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection. Your labs show mild inflammation—CRP and ESR are elevated—but white count is normal, and blood cultures are negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But the pain is really bad. I’ve been on dilaudid, but it’s not helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pain team reviewed your case. They suggest switching from dilaudid to oxycodone. Sometimes changing opioids helps. We’ll also increase your gabapentin to 900 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that. What about the prednisone? Should I go back up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your rheumatologist was consulted and recommends increasing prednisone to 40 mg daily for now. We’ll taper it slowly once you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I just want to get back to feeling stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also increase your lidocaine patches to three per day—wear them 12 hours on, 12 off. And we’ll keep monitoring your blood sugar since you’re on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been checking my sugars. They’ve been a bit high, but I adjust my Novolog based on what I eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep doing that. We’ll keep your other meds the same—metoprolol, lisinopril, statin, and CPAP at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. The oxycodone seems to be working better than the dilaudid. And I think the higher prednisone is helping too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your repeat labs are stable. No signs of kidney issues or infection. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if you keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Should I keep the lidocaine patches going after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three a day. And we’ll send you home with oxycodone for breakthrough pain—10 mg every four hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone? Do I stay on 40 mg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on 40 mg for now, but your rheumatologist will help you taper it down over the next few weeks. Don’t stop it suddenly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. What about my leg? Should I watch for redness or swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. The fluid collections are still there, but they’ve been culture-negative. No signs of infection now. But yes—watch for redness, warmth, or fever, and call your doctor if they appear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I had a little fall this morning going to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I heard. You hit your forehead. We ordered a head CT just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is everything okay? I didn’t lose consciousness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows no bleeding, no fracture. Just mild swelling on the scalp. You’re cleared. But we’ll make sure you have a walker for support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I think I need it—pain makes it hard to walk steadily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your condition is stable. We’re discharging you today. You’re alert, pain is controlled, and no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue prednisone 40 mg daily, oxycodone as needed, gabapentin 900 mg three times a day, and three lidocaine patches daily. Keep managing your diabetes with insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with my rheumatologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’ll help adjust your long-term treatment. Call them within the week. And if pain worsens or you develop fever, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me get through this flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping manage your care today. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad joint pain on my left side—elbow, fingers, knee, and foot. It’s been getting worse over the past five days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. This sounds similar to your last flare-up. Were you already increasing your prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, over the weekend I called the rheumatology team and raised it to 60 mg daily. Then on Monday, Dr. Evans told me to restart Imuran and go back to 40 mg prednisone, but the pain kept getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You were seen in clinic today and they decided to admit you so we could give IV steroids and better pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. I was also having a lot of diarrhea—up to 12 times in two hours this morning. It’s calmer now, but still concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s something we’re watching. Sometimes with severe arthritis flares, GI symptoms can flare too. We’re also checking to make sure it’s not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before during flares. But my doctor mentioned I might have IBD. Should we be testing for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We sent stool tests to rule out infections like C. diff, Salmonella, and parasites. All came back negative, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection. Does that mean it could be IBD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. But your diarrhea has already improved since admission, which suggests it’s linked to your arthritis flare. We’ll refer you to GI after discharge for further evaluation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my joint pain? It’s still pretty bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on IV methylprednisolone twice a day. That should help reduce inflammation faster than oral prednisone, especially since you’ve had diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so because I’ve had diarrhea, I might not be absorbing the pills well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s one reason we’re using IV steroids. We also started IV Dilaudid for pain and kept you on your usual gabapentin and MSContin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. The oxycodone wasn’t touching this pain. Is Imuran safe to restart? I remember it caused issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were restarted on it by your rheumatologist. We’re monitoring your blood work, but so far your labs look stable. It’s important for long-term control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. My left calf is also sore. Is that part of the flare or something else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping an eye on that. You’ve had fluid collections there before, but your exam shows no signs of infection now. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many admissions for that. I just hope it’s not another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your white count is only slightly elevated, and you’re not running a fever. That suggests inflammation, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my diabetes? My blood sugar was high in the ED.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your home insulin—Levemir and Novolog. Steroids can raise blood sugar, so we’ll check it regularly and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had that problem before with prednisone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. Honestly, I feel a bit better. The pain isn’t as intense, and I’ve only had two bowel movements overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. Your labs this morning show your white count is stable, and kidney function is normal. Blood sugar was a bit high at 221, but we adjusted your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So are we still thinking this is just a flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No signs of infection in your blood or stool. The improvement in both joint pain and diarrhea supports that this is a systemic flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the IV steroids for one more day, then transition you to a prednisone taper. Once your pain is controlled, we’ll switch back to oral pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be going home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you keep improving, yes. We want to make sure your pain is manageable and you’re not having more diarrhea before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like that. What about my rheumatology follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled to see Dr. Evans next week. He wants you to start Simponi, a new injectable medication, to help prevent future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of that. Is it better than the others I’ve tried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s another option that works differently. Since you’ve had reactions to other biologics, this might be a good fit. He’ll go over the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re doing well. You’re down to mild pain, and no diarrhea since last night. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual meds. The big change is a prednisone taper: 60 mg for four days, then 50, then 40, and stay there until you see Dr. Evans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll start Simponi next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Also, please follow up with your GI doctor to look into the diarrhea more, even though it’s improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep using your CPAP, monitor your blood sugar, and call if the pain worsens or you develop fever or new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home, and we’ll see you only in clinic—not here—next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having really bad joint pain on my left side—hand, knee, foot. It started after a bout of diarrhea, which finally cleared up, but the pain just got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned this followed diarrhea about a week ago. Has this pattern happened before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, every few weeks I get diarrhea, then joint pain follows. This time it’s much worse. I’m on 40 mg prednisone twice a day and my pain meds, but nothing’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your rheumatologist increased your steroids and MS Contin, but the pain isn’t controlled. That’s why you came in. I also see you’re having a headache and pain near your right ear?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the right side of my face is really sore. I had a bad parotid infection years ago, so I was worried it might be back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I checked, and there’s no swelling or fever, so it doesn’t look like an infection. But we’ll keep an eye on it. We’ll start you on IV steroids and pain medication to help get this flare under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I just need some relief. My hand is so swollen I can’t make a fist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Dilaudid in the ER, and we’ll continue with IV pain meds as needed. We also started IV methylprednisolone every 12 hours to reduce inflammation quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I stay on IV meds the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only until your pain improves. Once you’re stable, we’ll switch back to your oral medications. Your azathioprine is continuing as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes? I’ve been checking my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your Lantus insulin twice daily. You’ll keep counting carbs and using your Humalog as needed. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I was also wondering—my stool was orange-brown. Could that be blood?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That color can be from bile or diet, not necessarily blood. Since your diarrhea has resolved and you’re not anemic, we don’t suspect active GI bleeding. But we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your white count is slightly up, but no signs of infection. Your kidney function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the inflammation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. We also got your MRI results back. It shows mild tenosynovitis in your left hand—fluid around the tendons—but no joint damage or erosions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s inflammation, not permanent damage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s good news. It means this is an active flare, but your joints are still intact. The treatment should help calm it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. My pain is a bit better today, especially in my knee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’re going to stop the IV Dilaudid and switch to oxycodone for breakthrough pain. You’ll still have your regular MS Contin and tizanidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the steroids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re transitioning back to oral prednisone. You’ll go home on a taper—60 mg twice a day for five days, then down to 40 mg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to start tapering earlier, but the pain came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, flares can happen during tapers. That’s why we adjust. Just make sure to call your rheumatologist today to confirm the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. What about my other meds—like blood pressure and cholesterol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All continuing: lisinopril, HCTZ, metoprolol for blood pressure, and atorvastatin for cholesterol. We’re also keeping your alendronate for osteoporosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been consistent with those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I stopped by to check in. How’s the pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I’m still stiff, but I can move my fingers more. The headache is gone too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if things keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Will I need any new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. You’ll go home on the same meds you were on before, including the prednisone taper. Just start the 60 mg dose tomorrow as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your rheumatologist. They’ll monitor your disease control and may consider adjusting long-term therapy like Simponi.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. Your pain is much improved, and you’re walking independently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel like I can manage now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: start the prednisone taper today, keep managing your diabetes, and call your rheumatologist. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with severe joint pain. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Doctor. I have psoriatic arthritis, and three days ago I started having sudden pain and swelling in my left hand, knee, and elbow. I saw my rheumatologist, got a steroid shot in my hand, but it didn’t help. I even increased my prednisone to 80mg yesterday, but still no relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had no fever, chills, or other symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. But I’ve had some diarrhea the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. We’ll check that. Your vitals are stable, and your labs don’t show infection or inflammation markers. We’ve given you methylprednisolone and Dilaudid in the ER, which helped a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is this just another flare-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a flare, but we need to rule out infection. We’ll get X-rays of your hand and knee to check for fractures or joint damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your X-rays are back. No fractures or new bone damage. There’s significant soft tissue swelling in your hand and knee, which fits with your arthritis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But why isn’t the prednisone working this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes high-dose oral steroids aren’t enough during severe flares. We’re starting you on IV steroids to see if that helps better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a procedure called arthrocentesis—drawing fluid from your left knee. It helps relieve pressure and lets us check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll numb the area first. You’ll feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It’s important to rule out septic arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the joint fluid showed no white blood cells and no bacteria. No sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s definitely my arthritis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll continue IV steroids and your regular medications like azathioprine and gabapentin for pain and inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad in the knee. And now the skin around my knee is turning red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see some redness. Given your history of a leg abscess and being on immunosuppressants, we want to be cautious. We’ll do an ultrasound to check for any fluid collection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound shows no fluid collection or abscess near your old scar. The redness might be related to inflammation from the arthritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But it looks infected to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted infectious disease. Since you’re not running a fever and blood cultures are negative, it’s unlikely to be infection. The pattern of redness and now bruising suggests a skin reaction from inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative. No sign of bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re confident this is an inflammatory flare, not infection. We’ll keep monitoring the bruising on your knee and shin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an MRI of your knee today to check for complications like osteonecrosis, especially since you’re on high-dose steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but the MRI shows no osteonecrosis. However, there is a tear in the medial meniscus and significant degenerative changes in the knee joint.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. The focus is on controlling inflammation. The tear may contribute to swelling, but it’s not the main issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hand swelling is improving. But we’re still seeing bruising spread down your shin. It’s unusual, but consistent with severe inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried it’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your vitals are stable, no fever, and labs remain normal. This bruising is a reaction, not infection. We’re continuing your treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool test came back negative for C. diff. So your diarrhea isn’t from that, likely related to your IBS or medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I stop any meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll keep monitoring. Your diabetes and blood pressure are stable, so we’re continuing all home meds except adjusting pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The bruising has stopped spreading. That’s a good sign. Your knee swelling is slowly improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if things keep improving. You’ll need to continue a prednisone taper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on steroids so much. Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of the risks—like bone thinning and diabetes. That’s why we’re tapering slowly and continuing your alendronate and calcium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
